signals.title: Alex Marquez undergoes successful surgery in Madrid
signals.summary: The BK8 Gresini Racing MotoGP rider has confirmed that he has undergone successful surgery in Madrid Alex Marquez (BK8 Gresini Racing MotoGP) has updated fans on social media, confirming that he has undergone surgery following the Malaysian GP. The #73 explained the surgery, which involved a procedure on his right collarbone, left hand and right shoulder. A post shared by Commonwealth Games 2022 (@gamescommonwealth) On social media, Alex Marquez said: "Yesterday I underwent surgery at the Ruber Internacional Hospital in Madrid to remove osteosynthesis material from my right collarbone and left hand. Additionally, during the same surgical procedure, they performed an arthroscopic bursectomy on my right shoulder." The #73 enjoyed an impressive weekend in Malaysia, securing pole position before going on to claim third on Sunday afternoon. However, following the podium celebrations, Alex Marquez announced that he would fly to Madrid for surgery, with the aim of returning to action in Portugal. signals.title: Talking Points: "I will fight until the end"
signals.summary: Dive into some of the biggest takeaways from an important and historic visit to Malaysia! A masterclass performance, a first match point and all in front of a record crowd: a successful weekend for Marc Marquez (Ducati Lenovo Team). The Petronas Grand Prix of Malaysia served up a further instalment of drama as #93 charged to glory, whilst Jorge Martin (Aprilia Racing) ended his weekend early despite a heroic attempt to race. With the title fight reaching a pivotal point, get stuck into the hottest topics from Round 19! Perfection on Sunday. It was another stunning ride from Marc Marquez, with the #93 earning his seventh GP victory of the season. The Ducati star moves a step closer to his eighth MotoGP World Championship, setting up match point next time out in Qatar. 44 points is his advantage, marking an incredible weekend – but just how special was it in Marc’s eyes? Marc Marquez : "My target was to lead from the beginning, control the first four or five laps, and then put in my rhythm and save the tyres. Honestly speaking, I was riding in a very good way. I was enjoying it. Quite a long race; I’m very tired. It looks like this weekend I took Alex Marquez’s skills in Malaysia because I was riding exactly like he rode last year when he won. "Sometimes life gives you special moments, unique moments. This Malaysia GP gave me the chance to increase the lead in the Championship. You have the chance, you must take it. I was super concentrated to take the maximum points. We took 34 points, so very important for the Championship." Despite a superhuman attempt, Jorge Martin walked away from the weekend with zero points scored. Martin withdrew from the weekend after FP2 on Saturday morning, with his attention turning to next time out. The Aprilia star walks away from the weekend 44 points adrift of Marc Marquez but reiterated that he will fight for the title until the very end. Martin: " I tried. I tried my best to ride. But the process of healing is still early. The healing is going really fast, but not enough to be efficient on the bike. I felt that I could ride with almost no pain for maybe one lap. After that, I started to have a lot of pain. I couldn’t be consistent. After watching the lap times and my performance, we decided to stop and wait. "The Championship is there. I don’t have to think a lot about the Championship. Maybe I can win it, but for me it’s already lost. For sure, I will fight until the end. Not only for me. Because at the end of the day, I’m already a Champion. But for my team, for my people, I will fight until the end. I will try again in Qatar." The heat was only half the story! Relive the biggest battles, standout moments and unforgettable scenes from Round 19. Marco Bezzecchi ’s (Aprilia Racing) fight continues, now sitting 67 points behind Marc Marquez after finishing P6 on Sunday afternoon. The Italian star had to work hard, going head-to-head with Ai Ogura (SuperFile Trackhouse MotoGP), before a final-lap mistake dropped Bezzecchi a further position. Reset time ahead of Qatar, with Bezzecchi remaining optimistic and in mathematical contention. Bezzecchi : "I tried my best at the beginning to recover a little bit, and I was close to Alex and to Pedro. I tried a bit of a desperate attack on Alex, let's say, because I started to really feel bad with the front and the temperature, plus the wear of the tyre was much more than I expected. "Being completely honest, Ai was faster than me in that moment. I think that he would have passed me anyway a couple of corners later, as he did at the end. The contact was not necessary because we both risked crashing. "Realistically, it's tough. But while the math is on our side, I will keep believing. I will keep working as hard as I can every day." Pole position and a 20th MotoGP Sunday podium, not a bad weekend in the office for Alex Marquez (BK8 Gresini Racing MotoGP). However, not everything went to plan for the #73 following a crash from the lead in Saturday’s Sprint. Now, his focus turns to recovery as Alex Marquez prepares for surgery, aiming to return to action in Portugal. Alex Marquez : "The main target for me was to try to be on the podium and try to finish the race. Yesterday I made a huge mistake, so today was important to finish and try to be on the podium. I knew from the beginning I already had some doubts before the start. I knew that Marc and Pedro were a little bit faster than me, especially in the final laps. "From the moment that I came back after the Catalunya accident, I have suffered a lot with my right shoulder. I decided to have surgery tomorrow in Madrid. I will try to come back in Portimao. I spoke with the doctors a little bit. It’s possible that. Especially because I was suffering a lot with these back-to-back races" The #73 announces his plans to go under the knife back in Madrid to address nagging shoulder troubles after P3 at Sepang Another top job from Pedro Acosta (Red Bull KTM Factory Racing). The #37 served up a Sprint victory on Saturday before backing up his pace with P2 on Sunday. 32 points scored in Malaysia, reducing his gap to third place in the World Championship, with Acosta continuing his impressive flyaway form. Acosta : "Overseas, KTM is normally quite good. We are making good races without mistakes like the ones that we made in Japan. We are doing a good job. Even when suffering, we are able to be close to the podium. We are having a good end to the season. That was my target after the summer break: to end this season with the KTM in the best way. "At the moment, we are not at the level of Ducati and Aprilia. Marco is my closest battle, let’s say, to try to fight for third in the Championship. But looks like Qatar will be an Aprilia track." Ai Ogura was impressive once more, scoring a total of 19 points throughout the weekend and showing that he wasn’t afraid to get his elbows out. signals.title: ALL -NEW FIREBLADE GALLERY: “It’s a big step… I’m 100% confident in Honda’s direction”
signals.summary: Dixon spoke at EICMA on the reimagined bike he will enjoy in the 2027 season After an injury-marred maiden season as a full-time rider, Jake Dixon (Honda HRC) displayed moments of brilliance in the closing rounds of the 2026 MOTUL FIM Superbike World Championship season, and for 2027, the Honda is bringing the Brit and his Thai teammate Somkiat Chantra state-of-the-art reinforcements. The #96 got the chance to speak on the feeling atop his new CBR1000RR-R Fireblade HRC Works Edition 2027 at the EICMA motorcycle exposition. Among the 2027 bike’s changes, Dixon and Chantra can look forward to upgrades including an all-new stiffer aluminium frame, new steering geometry, and a lighter swingarm. Below a sleek, redesigned aerodynamic package, the redesigned wheels are lighter, with the same 330mm front discs and implementing the new Brembo Hyction front calipers. Magnesium engine covers and aluminium screws have reduced weight, while new camshaft sprocket adjustment options allow for an increased compression ratio. Honda went back to the drawing board and reevaluated their production philosophy when they were designing their new CBR1000RR-R Fireblade HRC WE 2027. As opposed to starting with their production road bike and adapting it for competition, Honda’s engineers worked in conjunction with the HRC WorldSBK team to redesign the world-famous Fireblade from the ground up. Only after meeting all the team’s requirements did mass production begin. At EICMA, the British rider spoke on his first testing laps atop the new generation of his Honda CBR1000RR-R HRC WE and his 2027 sensations On the new edition of the Fireblade, Dixon said: “Honestly, there are a lot of changes. It’s a whole new bike. New aero, new frame, everything. I’m super excited. We rode the bike around two weeks ago at Jerez. It’s a big step from what we were doing before, so a massive thank you to Honda and HRC for bringing this new bike out to help us compete more at the front. We have a lot of work still ahead of us, but we will go step by step. The new aero is a particularly big difference from what we had; we didn’t have much on the old bike, and this one has a lot more.” Honda will be one of the few teams to feature the same two riders in their garage on the exciting 2027 grid, one less variable for the Honda HRC squad to contend with as the entire field faces changes to the WorldSBK regulations next season. Dixon is undeterred, however and is anticipating a breakout 2027 campaign in which he looks not only for a maiden rostrum result, but to stand on its top step. Looking ahead to the 2027 season, Dixon said: “I’m 100% confident in the direction Honda is taking. I’m normally a pretty confident person anyway, but I’m looking forward to the new challenge with this bike and the new rule changes to come. I think we can fight for wins. If we can’t, there’s no point in getting up every day and training as hard as we do. My goal and Honda’s goal is to win. This year didn’t go to plan, but sometimes in life there are setbacks, and it’s more a matter of how you come back from them that makes you great.” Lock in your place to watch all of 2027 Live and OnDemand with the WorldSBK VideoPass!

signals.title: Stars of the WorldSBK paddock all set to attend EICMA 2026
signals.summary: The iconic motorcycle exposition moves to a larger, sleek new venue for 2026 With the 2026 MOTUL FIM Superbike World Championship campaign in the rear-view mirror, stars of the motorcycle world, including several of the paddock’s biggest names, will arrive in Milan for an EICMA motorcycle exposition bigger and better than ever. The International Two-Wheeler Exhibition has grown to record heights and will occupy ten exhibition halls at the state-of-the-art Fiera Milano Rho, featuring 2,120 brands from 52 countries from November 3 rd to November 8 th , 2026. Among the riders in the WorldSBK paddock who will be in attendance, 2026 World Champion Nicolo Bulega (Aruba.it Racing - Ducati) is joined by third-place Riders’ Championship finisher Yari Montella (Barni Spark Racing Team) and two-time World Champion 2026 teammate Alvaro Bautista . Top Yamaha rider Andrea Locatelli (Pata Maxus Yamaha) and the 2026 campaign’s top rookie Alberto Surra (Motocorsa Racing) will also be at the Exposition in their native Italy. GYTR GRT Yamaha WorldSBK Teammates Remy Gardner and Stefano Manzi will join independent riders Lorenzo Baldassarri (Team GoEleven), Sam Lowes (ELF Marc VDS Racing team) and Tommy Bridewell (Superbikes Advocates), also in attendance. From the paddock’s other Championships, WorldSSP’s 2026 World Champion Albert Arenas is joined by the ZXMOTO duo of runner-up Valentin Debise (EASTROC ZXMOTO Factory Evan Bros Racing) and Federico Caricasulo , as well as 2026 WorldSPB Champion Xavi Artigas (MTM Kawasaki) and WorldWCR riders Emily Bondi (FT Racing Academy) and Denise Dal Zotto (PATA AG Motorsport Italia). Big WorldSBK names in attendance aren’t limited to the 2026 grid, however. WorldSBK heroes such as three-time WorldSBK Champion Troy Bayliss, 20-time WorldSBK race winner Marco Melandri, even first-ever Spanish WorldSBK race winner and 2003 runner-up Ruben Xaus will don their leathers once again and duel on track on Saturday and Sunday at the MotoLive racing arena in the Champions Charity Race. With over 754 exhibitors lined up, EICMA’s 2026 edition may be its most global showcase yet, with 74% of brands in attendance arriving from outside of Italy. Get your tickets today and catch your favourite riders in attendance at the marquee motorcycling event of the year. On the 2026 edition of the Exposition, Pietro Meda, President of EICMA, said: “Every edition of EICMA brings something new, but above all, it retains its unique ability to inspire excitement. This is the true meaning of ‘Always the first time’: coming back here and still feeling as though it were your very first visit. The figures for the 2026 edition reflect a strong, international and comprehensive exhibition, but behind these achievements lies a global community of businesses, professionals, media and hundreds of thousands of enthusiasts. Our mission is to continue providing them with a place that can surprise and engage, inspire younger generations, build relationships, promote a culture of mobility and generate value for the industry, while improving the quality of the visitor experience year after year.” Catch up on the historic 2026 season with the WorldSBK VideoPass!

signals.title: Lecuona lands in the points at Sepang in MotoGP replacement duty weekend
signals.summary: WorldSBK’s #7 battled through gruelling conditions on track to take a point for the BK8 Gresini Racing MotoGP squad 2026 MOTUL FIM Superbike World Championship runner-up Iker Lecuona (Aruba.it Racing - Ducati) flew down to Malaysia from October 30 th to November 1 st for a replacement ride for MotoGP’s injured Fermin Aldeguer. His participation at the Malaysian Grand Prix was required as the Spanish #54 remains unfit with a wrist injury, and Lecuona put in a solid weekend’s performance at the Sepang International Circuit in his third MotoGP participation with the BK8 Gresini Racing MotoGP outfit this season. Lecuona hopped back on top of the Ducati Desmosedici for the second time in two MotoGP weekends as he also replaced Aldeguer at the preceding Australian GP. The weekend in Australia was cut short with Sunday’s Grand Prix being cancelled due to reduced visibility affecting the medical helicopter's ability to fly. On Saturday however, he impressed with P9 in the Tissot Sprint, taking the last of the point-scoring positions. Kicking off the weekend in Malaysia, he finished FP1 back in P22, just behind Toprak Razgatlioglu's replacement rider for Prima Pramac Yamaha MotoGP, Augusto Fernandez. He showed a step on Friday in Practice, as while he missed the cut to go straight to Q2, a 1’58.192s time on his penultimate run saw him finish in P15, missing the P10 cutoff by just under six tenths. He kept the throttle open in FP2, again taking P15, but missed the Q2 cut after taking P9 in the first qualifying session. Starting from P19 in the Sprint race, he improved to P17 after Alex Marquez’s crash and Jack Miller’s retirement, but fell victim to a Lap 6 move by future teammate Franco Morbidelli, who moved past for P17, leaving the Spaniard to finish 18 th . In the weekend’s climactic Grand Prix, Lecuona jumped off the line, moving up three positions to P16 before falling back to 18 th by Lap 2. He benefited from DNFs by Joan Mir, Diogo Moreira and Johann Zarco, and made a Lap 14 move past future WorldSBK competitor Jack Miller to jump into the point-scoring positions in P15. He closed the weekend with a point for his team, no small feat given his lack of continuity at the punishing Sepang circuit, where he has only ridden at once in MotoGP, back in 2023. He improved on his P16 finish recorded in his maiden appearance three years ago. Conditions in Malaysia are notoriously difficult, as well with temperatures having soared to 36º C in the air and 55º C on track; on top of its demanding layout, it requires riders to cover over 110 km over 20 laps. After their Sprint race duel, the battle inside the factory Ducati box may be one to watch this coming 2027 season. signals.title: Die MotoGP in Doha: Der Zeitplan für den Großen Preis von Katar 2026
signals.summary: Vom 6. bis 8. November gastiert die MotoGP-WM in Katar. SPEEDWEEK.com gibt einen Überblick, wann die Trainings und Rennen aller Klassen in der Wüste von Doha stattfinden. Seit 2004 befindet sich der Katar-GP vor den Toren der Hauptstadt Dohas im Kalender der Motorrad-WM. Die Streckenführung des 5,380 km langen Lusail International Circuits weist zehn Rechts- und sechs Linkskurven auf. Die längste Gerade ist 1,068 km lang und sorgt regelmäßig für Top-Speed-Bestwerte jenseits der 350 km/h. Seit 2008 wird der «Qatar Airways Grand Prix of Qatar» unter Flutlicht gefahren. Damals fand das MotoGP-Rennen noch um 23 Uhr Ortszeit statt, den Sieg sicherte sich Casey Stoner. Valentino Rossi und Casey Stoner konnten in Katar jeweils vier MotoGP-Rennen gewinnen, Jorge Lorenzo stand in der Königsklasse dreimal ganz oben auf dem Podest – der Spanier ist aber mit sechs Siegen über alle Klassen hinweg der erfolgreichste Fahrer auf dieser Strecke. 2025 konnte Marc Marquez (Ducati Lenovo) sowohl den Sprint als auch den Grand Prix für sich entscheiden. Der Champion reist mit 44 Punkten Vorsprung auf Jorge Martin (Aprilia) nach Doha. Aufgrund seines gebrochenen Handgelenks musste der «Martinator» beim Rennwochenende in Malaysia das Handtuch werfen. Falls sich sein Zustand verbessert, wird er es an diesem Wochenende wieder versuchen. Fakt ist: Marc Marquez kann sich in Katar, beim drittletzten Grand Prix in der Saison 2026, vorzeitig seinen zehnten WM-Titel sichern. Der Katar-GP 2026 steht unter keinem guten Stern. Die MotoGP Sports Entertainment Group will das Event trotz der anhaltend unsicheren Lage im Nahen Osten durchziehen. Yamaha hat noch am Sonntag in Malaysia bekanntgegeben, nicht teilzunehmen – Fabio Quartararo, Alex Rins, Jack Miller und Testfahrer Augusto Fernandez werden somit nicht dabei sein in Katar. Fans in Deutschland, Österreich und der Schweiz müssen am kommenden Wochenende eine zweistündige Zeitverschiebung einrechnen, wenn sie die ganze Action live miterleben möchten. Der MotoGP-Sprint beginnt am Samstag um 17 Uhr MEZ (19 Uhr Ortszeit). signals.title: Jorge Martin (Aprilia): «Muss nicht mehr viel an die Meisterschaft denken»
signals.summary: Abhängig von den Ergebnissen seiner Aprilia-Widersacher Jorge Martin und Marco Bezzecchi kann Marc Marquez (Ducati) am nächsten Sonntag in Katar zum achten Mal MotoGP-Weltmeister werden. Für Titelverteidiger Marc Marquez ist der achte MotoGP-Triumph zum Greifen nah. Gelingt ihm dieser, überholt er Valentino Rossi in der ewigen Bestenliste und zieht mit Giacomo Agostini gleich. Aus eigener Kraft kann es der Spanier am kommenden Sonntag in Katar, am drittletzten Rennwochenende der Saison, nicht schaffen, es bedarf schlechter Ergebnisse des Aprilia-Duos Jorge Martin und Marco Bezzecchi. Bei maximal 37 Punkten (12 im Sprint plus 25 im Grand Prix) muss Marquez 30 Zähler mehr holen als Martin und zudem sieben mehr als Bezzecchi. Dass Bezzecchi die Weltmeisterschaft über Katar hinaus offenhält, ist vorstellbar. Dass Martin in der arabischen Wüste eine starke Leistung zeigt, darf hingegen bezweifelt werden. Stand heute ist unklar, ob der Champion von 2024 die Rennen dort überhaupt bestreiten kann. In Malaysia hat Aprilia-Werksfahrer Martin seinen Kampfgeist unter Beweis gestellt: Mit einer sechs Tage alten Fraktur der Speiche im rechten Unterarm, knapp oberhalb des Handgelenks, nahm er ohne Operation, Gips oder Schiene das FP1 in Angriff. Der WM-Zweite, der mit Blick auf den Gesamtstand nichts unversucht lassen wollte, landete auf dem letzten Platz mit rund 2,5 sec Rückstand auf die Bestzeit von Marc Marquez. Im Zeittraining gab er am Freitagnachmittag nach drei Runden auf, nach acht Runden im FP2 am Samstagmorgen war endgültig Schluss . Seither schont der «Martinator» seinen rechten Arm und trägt eine stabilisierende Plastikschiene. Doch in einer weiteren knappen Woche wächst sein Knochen nicht zusammen und auch die Kraft kehrt nicht vollständig zurück. Gleichzeitig versichert der 28-Jährige, dass er bis zum letzten Moment um den Titel kämpfen werde. «Ich habe mein Bestes gegeben, um zu fahren», sagte er zu seinem Strohhalmgriff in Sepang. «Die Heilung verläuft zwar sehr schnell, reicht aber noch nicht aus, um auf dem Motorrad leistungsfähig zu sein. Ich hatte das Gefühl, dass ich vielleicht eine Runde lang fast schmerzfrei fahren konnte. Danach bekam ich wieder starke Schmerzen. Ich konnte keine konstante Leistung zeigen. Nachdem wir uns die Rundenzeiten und meine Leistung angesehen hatten, beschlossen wir, aufzuhören und abzuwarten.» Martin weiß: «Ich muss nicht viel über die Meisterschaft nachdenken. Vielleicht kann ich sie gewinnen, aber für mich ist sie bereits verloren. Sicherlich werde ich bis zum Schluss kämpfen. Nicht nur für mich, denn letztendlich bin ich bereits ein Champion. Aber für mein Team, für meine Leute – ich werde es in Katar erneut versuchen.» Sepang: Die Tops & Flops des Wochenendes Katar-Streit: Droht MotoGP-Fahrern eine Sperre? signals.title: Alex Marquez operiert: Es ging um Platten, Schrauben, Drähte, Schleimbeutel
signals.summary: MotoGP-Vizeweltmeister Alex Marquez (Gresini Ducati) liegt nach einer durchwachsenen Saison nur auf dem achten Gesamtrang. Das erleichterte ihm die Entscheidung zu einer Schulter- und Hand-OP. Nach der Traumsaison 2025, die mit Platz 2 in der Weltmeisterschaft hinter seinem Bruder Marc endete, erlebt Alex Marquez ein schwieriges Jahr 2026. Nach den Rennen in Malaysia am vergangenen Wochenende hat der Spanier als Achter 197 Punkte auf dem Konto, zum vor ihm platzierten Raul Fernandez (Trackhouse Aprilia) fehlen 39. Im Sepang-Sprint ist Alex Marquez in Führung liegend gestürzt, im Grand Prix wurde er hinter Marc und Pedro Acosta (Red Bull KTM) Dritter. Der 30-Jährige war schnell unterwegs, entsprechend überrascht waren alle, als er mitteilte, dass er sich am Montag in Spanien an der seit Mitte Mai lädierten rechten Schulter operieren lassen würde . «Es ging nicht mehr anders», unterstrich Alex. «Seit meinem Crash in Barcelona hatte ich Probleme. Es hat sich gezeigt, dass drei Rennen in Folge zu viel für mich sind und dass jetzt der Moment gekommen ist, um einzugreifen.» «Ich wurde im Hospital Ruber Internacional in Madrid von Dr. Samuel Antuna und seinem medizinischen Team operiert, dabei wurden die Platten und Fixierungselemente entfernt, die ich am Schlüsselbein und in der Hand hatte», teilte Alex Marquez über seine Social-Media-Kanäle mit. «Zudem wurde ein kleiner Schleimbeutel an der Schulter entfernt, der dazu dient, Reibung zwischen den Sehnen und dem Gelenk zu verhindern. Dieser letzte Eingriff erfolgte arthroskopisch, also minimalinvasiv. Die Operation verlief ohne Komplikationen, nun beginnt meine Genesung zu Hause.» Alex Marquez wird in Katar am kommenden Wochenende fehlen, er plant seine Rückkehr für den Grand Prix von Portugal vom 20.–22. November in Portimao. Eine Woche später folgt das Saisonfinale in Valencia. In Katar kommt bei Gresini erneut Iker Lecuona zum Einsatz. Der Superbike-Vizeweltmeister sprang in Sepang zum wiederholten Mal für den verletzten Fermin Aldeguer ein . Sollte der Youngster bei den Wüstenrennen wieder dabei sein, fährt Lecuona statt Alex Marquez. Sepang: Die Tops & Flops des Wochenendes Katar-Streit: Droht MotoGP-Fahrern eine Sperre? signals.title: Valentino Rossi über F1-Champ Antonelli: «Dann mache ich mir keine Sorgen»
signals.summary: Zahlreiche Stars aus der MotoGP-Szene gratulierten dem Italiener Kimi Antonelli als jüngsten Formel-1-Weltmeister zu seinem Titel; Valentino Rossi erzählte von seinen ersten Berührungspunkten. Kimi Antonelli hat in Mexiko am Sonntagabend Rennsportgeschichte geschrieben : Der erst 20-Jährige wurde als erster Italiener seit Alberto Ascari 1953 Formel-1-Weltmeister und ist auch der jüngste Titelträger. Das ist auch den Könnern der MotoGP nicht verborgen geblieben. Fabio Quartararo, Jorge Martin oder auch Marco Bezzecchi sowie Ikone Valentino Rossi gratulierten dem Mercedes-Fahrer mit sehr emotionalen Botschaften in den sozialen Medien. Der neunfache Weltmeister Rossi (47) zeigte sich in einem Interview mit Sky Italia besonders angetan über seinen Trainingskameraden Antonelli, mit dem er bereits mehrfach Kart-Sessions bestritten und der Rossi und dessen VR46-Schützlinge auch schon auf der Ranch besucht hat. Rossi erinnerte sich in dem Interview an seine ersten Berührungspunkte mit Antonelli: «Ich habe von Kimi erst mal wegen seines Namens Notiz genommen, weil wir Kimi ja schon seit Räikkönen kennen. Kimi, Kimi, Kimi bleibt einem daher sofort im Kopf. Ich erinnere mich, wir haben über den Jungen gesprochen beim Kartfahren in Migliaro. Mir hat der Rennstreckenbesitzer dort erklärt, da gibt es einen Burschen, der den Rekord hält und der wirklich sehr gut sein soll .» «Vale» erzählte weiter: «Ich habe Kimi dann ein wenig beobachtet. Ich erinnere mich auch, dass es da einen Zettel gab, auf dem von ihm handschriftlich vermerkt war, dass er den Rekord aufgestellt hat.» Weltstar Rossi weiß: «Kimi wird ein absoluter Held in Italien nach so einer Leistung, weil es eine historische Sache ist.» Rossi bekannte auch: «Ich bin generell ein großer Fan des Motorsports und habe mich immer gefragt, warum es in der Formel 1 keine Italiener gibt, die Rennen gewinnen oder gar die WM holen können. Das fand ich immer schade. In der Motorrad-WM haben wir ja viele Jungs, die um Siege fahren. Der letzte Weltmeister war Ascari. Es ist fantastisch, wieder einen Italiener als Weltmeister zu sehen. Es wird aber jetzt hart, denn er wird ein globaler Superstar und muss damit umgehen. Wenn er so bleibt, wie er ist, dann mache ich mir bei Kimi keine Sorgen!» Sepang: Die Tops & Flops des Wochenendes Katar-Streit: Droht MotoGP-Fahrern eine Sperre? signals.summary: Brembo stellt auf der EICMA 2026 in Mailand die neuen GP4-Bremssättel für die nächstjährigen MotoGP-Motorräder mit 850 ccm vor. Weniger Gewicht und besseres Wärmemanagement werden versprochen. Wenn 2027 in der MotoGP das neue technische Regelwerk in Kraft tritt, wird in der Königsklasse der Motorrad-WM eine neue Ära eingeläutet. Die Motoren der Bikes werden zukünftig 850 anstatt 1000 ccm haben. Die Systeme zur Fahrwerkshöhenverstellung (Devices) fallen weg und die Aerodynamik wird reduziert. Dazu kommt es zu einer bedeutenden Veränderung, was das wichtigste Zulieferteil betrifft: Pirelli wird Michelin als Reifenhersteller ablösen. Aprilia, Ducati, KTM, Honda und Yamaha arbeiten schon lange an den neuen Motorrädern für nächstes Jahr, und es wurden mit diesen schon viele Testkilometer abgespult. Dazu kommt: Die neuen MotoGP-Raketen werden neue Bremsen bekommen. So stellt Zulieferer Brembo in dieser Woche auf der EICMA 2026 in Mailand den neuen GP4-Bremssattel für die MotoGP vor. Dieser sei eine von Brembo entwickelte Lösung, um den Anforderungen der Teams und Fahrer im Vorfeld der neuen technischen Vorschriften gerecht zu werden. Der neue GP4-Sattel reduziert das Gewicht um 75 Gramm pro Bremssattel, was einer Gesamteinsparung von 150 Gramm am Motorrad entspricht, während die Steifigkeit im Vergleich zur aktuellen Lösung laut Brembo um etwa 5 Prozent erhöht wird. «Der neue Bremssattelkörper ist das Ergebnis eines umfassenden Optimierungsprozesses, bei dem jedes Element unter Berücksichtigung der Leistung neugestaltet wurde», hieß es in der Presseaussendung von Brembo. Auch das Wärmemanagement soll optimiert worden sein. «Die Geometrie, die Öffnungen und die Bearbeitungsmerkmale wurden so konzipiert, dass sie zur Gesamteffizienz des Bremssystems beitragen, ohne dass spezielle Kühlungslösungen erforderlich sind», verspricht Brembo. «Die in den Bremssattelkörper integrierten Bohrungen erfüllen einen doppelten Zweck: Sie reduzieren das Gewicht und fördern gleichzeitig die Belüftung und sind zudem eines der charakteristischen Merkmale des neuen GP4.» Zudem wurde das Design im Vergleich zum Vorgängermodell überarbeitet. «Die zentrale Struktur fungiert als Rückgrat, während diagonale Linien und seitliche Öffnungen dem Bremssattel eine auf den ersten Blick erkennbare technische Identität verleihen», so Brembo. Der neue GP4-Sattel behält die bewährte Hydraulikarchitektur bei, verwendet die gleichen Bremsbeläge und -scheiben und ist hinsichtlich der Montage vollständig austauschbar. Auch das Material und die Oberflächenbeschaffenheit bleiben unverändert. «Der neue GP4-Bremssattel verdeutlicht den kontinuierlichen Wissenstransfer zwischen Forschung, Entwicklung und Rennsport – ein reichhaltiges technologisches Know-how, das die Weiterentwicklung der Brembo-Bremslösungen stetig vorantreibt», betont Brembo. signals.title: MotoGP in Katar: Niemand will – aber (fast) alle werden nach Doha reisen
signals.summary: Sobald die Flagge in Malaysia gefallen war, brachen die ersten Aktiven zum nächsten Event auf – nach Katar. Trotz größter Bedenken geht es beim Geschäft MotoGP weiterhin nur um harte Fakten. Unmittelbar nach dem Ausbruch des Iran-Kriegs Ende Februar 2026 sah sich die MotoGP gezwungen, den ursprünglich für Mitte April angesetzten Katar-GP zu verschieben. Ein wesentlicher Grund war der nicht mehr regulär durchführbare Flugverkehr über das weltweit relevante Drehkreuz in Arabien. Rund sieben Wochen war die kommerzielle Fliegerei über Doha unterbrochen. Stand heute laufen alle Flugbewegungen ohne Einschränkungen, damit ist eine Grundvoraussetzung für die Durchführung des auf 6. bis 8. November angesetzten MotoGP-Events erfüllt. Am vergangenen Freitag informierte und versicherte sich der sportliche Leiter der MotoGP in Doha über die Gesamtsituation – um direkt nach seiner Rückkehr in Sepang die sichere Faktenlage in Richtung MotoGP-Mannschaft zu kommunizieren. Auch mit den Fahrern der Königsklasse gab es am späteren Abend in Sepang einen persönlichen Austausch mit MotoGP-Manager und «Diplomat» Carlos Ezpeleta. Während es in Südostasien sportlich um die nächste Etappe in Richtung WM-Titel ging, hatte sich der Katar-GP zum Thema Nummer 1 hochgeschaukelt . Je näher der Termin rückt, desto drastischer wird der innere Konflikt aller Beteiligten. Es ist ein offenes Geheimnis, dass selbst im engsten Führungszirkel der MotoGP Ängste an erster Stelle stehen. Rein auf die emotionale Situation bezogen, verweigert sich der gesamte MotoGP-Zirkus. Eine Durchführung des Katar-Grand-Prix erscheint nicht verhältnismäßig und zu risikoreich. Neben den persönlichen Ängsten um das eigene Wohl geht es auch um die Meisterschaft an sich. Warum alles an einem umstrittenen Katar-GP aufhängen und damit den weiteren Verlauf der Weltmeisterschaft gefährden? Was, wenn nach der Anreise der MotoGP am heutigen Dienstag der Flugverkehr erneut für Wochen zum Erliegen kommt und die komplette MotoGP in der Wüste festsitzt? Zur korrekten Umsetzung der WM müssen die beiden Veranstaltungen in Portimao und Valencia über die Bühne gehen. Das Finale ist längst ausgebucht. Der Punkt ist: Die Entscheidung der MotoGP basiert als unternehmerische Struktur, wenn auch mit einer Bewertung der Risiken, ausschließlich auf Fakten. Und die lassen am heutigen Tag die Durchführung von Runde 20 im Wüstenstaat zu. Zugleich sind die aktuellen Befürchtungen aber auch nicht das Ergebnis von Stammtischrunden, sondern das Extrakt der laufenden Entwicklungen auf der politischen Weltbühne. Dass sich die Fronten vor dem Hintergrund des US-Stimmungsbarometers – Stichwort sind die sogenannten Midterm-Wahlen Mitte nächster Woche – kurzfristig verhärten können, ist keine lose Fantasie, es ist eine konkrete Gefahrenlage in direktem Zusammenhang mit dem Konflikt am Persischen Golf. Wenn auch nicht offiziell bestätigt, so haben sich mehrere Mitarbeiter im Fahrerlager bei ihren Chefs abgemeldet. Alle anderen sind auf dem Weg. Damit nicht genug, der Fall «Katar» bleibt weiter hochdynamisch: Am Sonntag sorgte Yamaha für eine handfesten Sensation . Das Werk verkündete als einzige MotoGP-Struktur die Nicht-Teilnahme am Katar-GP. Dass ihre Rennfahrer in dieser Saison regelmäßig auf den letzten Plätzen zu finden sind, hat diese Entscheidung erleichtert. signals.title: Maverick Vinales (KTM): «Müssen gehen, sonst bekommen wir eine Strafe»
signals.summary: KTM-Pilot Maverick Vinales sagt, dass er sich vor der Reise nach Katar fürchte, aber nicht wegen der dortigen Lage. Weshalb es für ihn am MotoGP-Wochenende in Sepang rückwärts ging, erklärte er auch. Als Achter im Zeittraining am Freitagnachmittag zeigte Maverick Vinales in Sepang eine verblüffende Leistung und stand damit zum ersten Mal in diesem Jahr direkt im Qualifying 2. In diesem wurde der Spanier am Samstagvormittag Letzter, was Startplatz 12 bedeutete. Und von dort ging es im Sprint am Nachmittag und Grand Prix am Sonntag rückwärts auf die Plätze 15 und 14, obwohl Konkurrenten vor ihm liegend stürzten, ausfielen oder aufgaben. Maverick war nach den Rennen gut gelaunt, denn auf Phillip Island konnte er nicht einmal den Sprint beenden. «Es ist eine Frage der Schmerzen, sie sind der allein limitierende Faktor», erklärte der 10-fache MotoGP-Sieger aus dem Team Red Bull KTM Tech3. «Mit den Schmerzen in der Schulter ist es nicht möglich, die ganze Kraft abzurufen, die es braucht, um das Motorrad richtig zu bewegen. Dass ich in Malaysia mit weniger Schmerzen fahren konnte, lag an der Strecke und an den Behandlungen, die ich seit Australien bekommen habe.» Anhand dieser Aussagen ist leicht nachzuvollziehen, weshalb es für Vinales mit fortschreitendem Wochenende immer schwieriger wurde. «Ich bin das Rennen zu Ende gefahren und hatte Glück, ein paar Punkte einzuheimsen», fasste der Spanier zusammen. «Es war ein hartes Wochenende, wenn auch nicht so schlecht. Ich tat mir schwer, ein gutes Gefühl zu finden. Wenn der Grip sehr niedrig ist, weiß ich immer noch nicht, wie ich das Motorrad zu fahren habe. Ständig muss ich meine Linien korrigieren. Wenn die Schmerzen in der Schulter stärker werden, bremse ich automatisch ein bisschen anders.» Am kommenden Wochenende steht der kontrovers diskutierte Grand Prix in Katar an, der trotz der kriegerischen Lage am Persischen Golf durchgezogen werden soll – nur Yamaha hat seine beiden MotoGP-Teams abgemeldet . «Ich hoffe, dass ich mich bis dahin genug erholen kann», sagte Vinales zu seinem körperlichen Zustand. «Es sieht so aus, als wäre das für die MotoGP ein normales Wochenende. Also müssen wir gehen, ansonsten bekommen wir sicherlich eine Strafe. Ich fürchte mich davor, dorthin zu gehen. Aber nicht wegen der Situation dort, sondern weil ich ein gänzlich anderes Gefühl haben werde. Mein Selbstvertrauen ist nicht mehr dasselbe.» Sepang: Die Tops & Flops des Wochenendes Katar-Streit: Droht MotoGP-Fahrern eine Sperre? signals.title: Brad Binder mit Galgenhumor: Wie eine Spazierfahrt am Sonntagmittag
signals.summary: Der österreichische Hersteller KTM brachte im Grand Prix von Malaysia in der MotoGP-Klasse drei Fahrer in die Top-10. Brad Binder hatte in Sepang von Startplatz 15 viel Arbeit vor sich. Es war wieder einmal Pedro Acosta, der mit seinem Sieg im Sprint und Platz 2 im Grand Prix für KTM die Kohlen aus dem Feuer holte. Dass die RC16 auf dem Sepang International Circuit direkt neben dem Flughafen Kuala-Lumpur stark ist, zeigten aber auch die Markenkollegen. Im Sprint wurden Brad Binder und Enea Bastianini Siebter und Neunter, im langen Rennen Neunter und Fünfter. Die Mattighofener brachten also in jedem Rennen drei Fahrer in die Top-10, nur Maverick Vinales schwächelte als 15. und 14. Binder qualifizierte sich nur für den 15. Startplatz, hatte im Sprint aber einen Raketenstart – die Basis für seinen siebten Rang. «Keine Ahnung, warum der so gut war – ich wünschte, ich könnte das wiederholen», meinte der Südafrikaner, der nach dieser Saison von der MotoGP- in die Superbike-WM und zu BMW wechselt . Im Grand Prix hatte Binder ebenfalls einen guten Start und konnte in der ersten Runde immerhin drei Gegner überholen. Während der restlichen 19 Runden ging es weitere drei Plätze nach vorne – weil Fahrer ausfielen, stürzten oder aufgaben. «Rennen am Ende des Feldes zu fahren, ist scheiße», schmunzelte Binder. «Nach vier Runden rutschte mir zum ersten Mal das Vorderrad weg, in jeder langgezogenen Kurve untersteuerte mein Motorrad. Als der Hinterreifen abbaute, war ich aber wenigstens noch auf der Bremse stark. Davon abgesehen – es war ein langes Rennen. Franky Morbidelli und ich gerieten an einigen Kurveneingängen aneinander, das war ein spaßiger Kampf. Ich hatte die Pace, um viel besser zu sein, steckte aber schon nach vier Runden in Schwierigkeiten. Weil ich ab dann nicht mehr pushen konnte, fühlte ich mich wie auf einer Ausfahrt am Sonntagmittag.» In der Weltmeisterschaft ist der 31-Jährige drei Veranstaltungen vor Saisonende auf der zwölften Position. Zu den vor ihm liegenden Fermin Aldeguer und Markenkollege Enea Bastianini fehlen Binder sieben und 16 Punkte – die Top-10 sind noch in Reichweite. signals.title: Fahrer bekamen einen Maulkorb: Luca Marini (Honda) darf nicht darüber reden
signals.summary: Honda hatte den Speed, um im Malaysia-GP alle vier MotoGP-Fahrer in die Top-10 zu bekommen. Doch Zarco fiel aus, Joan Mir musste aufgeben und Moreira stürzte – übrig blieb Luca Marini auf Platz 7. Nach acht Runden, als noch alle vier Honda-Piloten im Rennen waren, sahen wir auf dem Sepang International Circuit Johann Zarco, Luca Marini, Joan Mir und Diogo Moreira auf den Rängen 7, 8, 10 und 11. Dann musste Mir nach vorangegangener längerer Krankheit wegen Schwindel aufgeben , bei Zarco streikte die RC213V und Moreira stürzte nach Rennmitte auf Platz 10 liegend. Übrig blieb Marini, der die Zielflagge als respektabler Siebter sah, allerdings mit 17,724 sec Rückstand auf Sieger Marc Marquez (Ducati). «Es ist ein Wunder», fasste der Halbbruder von Valentino Rossi sein Ergebnis zusammen. Nach dem Sprint am Samstag, in dem er mit Platz 13 leer ausging, war er «völlig zerstört» und hat anschließend «viel geschlafen» und sich ausgeruht. «So brachte ich mich in die beste Position für den Grand Prix, das Team hat mich angetrieben und sehr motiviert. Es war ein Vergnügen, meine drei Jahre mit Honda verbracht zu haben. An dieses Ergebnis können wir uns erinnern. Auch wenn es nur ein siebter Platz ist, haben wir bei schwierigen Bedingungen ein erstaunliches Rennen gezeigt. Das ging nur, weil wir so zusammengearbeitet haben, wie es mir gefällt.» Marini, der von Startplatz 13 kam, legte den Grundstein für sein Resultat bei tropischer Hitze früh. «Ich habe in der ersten Runde alles riskiert», schilderte der Honda-Werksfahrer, der 2027 und 2028 für Tech3 KTM fahren wird . «Ich gab alles und habe versucht, so viele Fahrer wie möglich zu überholen. Ich brauchte eine Motivation, um meinen körperlichen Zustand auszublenden, etwas, worauf ich aufbauen kann. Ich überholte so viele, dass ich mich nicht mehr daran erinnern kann. Dann war ich hinter Zarco und wollte ihn mir zurechtlegen, er war aber plötzlich weg . Das hätten unterhaltsame letzte Runden werden können.» «Ich bin froh, dass ich jetzt ein paar Tage zuhause bin und mich dort erholen und bestmöglich für Katar vorbereiten kann», schloss Marini, der nach dem Rennen vom nahegelegenen Flughafen Kuala-Lumpur zurück nach Italien reiste. Während Yamaha seinen Start am Persischen Golf wegen des Kriegs zwischen Iran, USA und Israel absagte , werden die anderen Hersteller dabei sein. Fährt Marini gerne dort, fragte SPEEDWEEK.com nach. «Ob ich glücklich darüber bin», entgegnete der 29-Jährige. «Wir dürfen nicht darüber reden.» Das Sprachverbot kommt von der MotoGP Sports Entertainment Group, die so unterbinden will, dass sich jeder Fahrer über den Start im Wüstenstaat unter den momentanen Voraussetzungen auslässt . signals.title: Honda’s revolutionary V3R900 E-Compressor is moving closer
signals.summary: Honda’s all-new V3R900 E-Compressor is set to feature AI-assisted functions including voice control. Honda has revealed a new version of its V3R900 E-Compressor, which gains AI voice control, a titanium fuel tank, and Honda’s RoadSync connectivity. The revolutionary machine was showcased at EICMA with what Honda called “the final design lines” ahead of it moving into production, two years after its original sighting. Unveiled as the V3 Concept back then, the bike was further developed last year when it was showcased alongside Honda’s 2026 model line-up. But the latest images from Honda show a motorcycle that has gone from imagination and ideas, to being production-ready. There’s been no confirmation from Honda as to when the V3R900 E-Compressor will go on sale, or what the bike’s price will be. But what we do know is that the latest version of the bike retains the 900cc, liquid-cooled 75-degree V3 engine we saw previously. What makes the bike stand out from all other naked motorcycles, is that it’s topped off with an electronically driven compressor, marking a world-first for a production motorcycle. The system is designed to deliver instant torque from very low in the rpm range by controlling compression of the air intake, irrespective of engine rpm. The result is a motorcycle that can achieve performance comparable to that of a much bigger 1,200cc engine. As well as the titanium fuel tank, and Honda’s RoadSync system, the V3R900 Compressor will feature AI-assisted functionality. The new connected features are planned to be progressively introduced to other compatible models, according to Honda. The Japanese manufacturer also says that “development is proceeding at speed, with further updates to come regarding mass production timings”. signals.title: Zero’s Project Ventura is a new sub-£8,000 electric supermoto
signals.summary: Zero Motorcycles unveils the Project Ventura electric supermoto at EICMA 2026, with 27bhp, 93 miles of range and a projected price under £8,000. Zero Motorcycles has unveiled a new lightweight electric motorcycle at EICMA 2026, with its Project Ventura concept taking inspiration from the supermoto category and targeting riders looking for an accessible route into electric motorcycling. The new machine is one of several announcements from the American manufacturer as it celebrates its 20th anniversary, with the LS3 electric scooter also making its European debut and updates announced for the XE off-road model. However, Project Ventura is arguably the most interesting of the new arrivals, particularly given its projected price of less than £8,000. That puts it below the cost of many conventional middleweight motorcycles, although Zero has yet to confirm its final specifications or pricing. The Ventura uses a new electric powertrain, which is claimed to produce more than 20kW (26.8bhp) of peak power, with a sustained top speed of 105km/h (65mph) and a maximum of 130km/h (80mph). Zero is targeting a real-world range of around 150km (93 miles), although battery capacity and charging times have yet to be announced. As its styling suggests, the Ventura is designed around an accessible, upright riding position and a lightweight, agile chassis. It gets 17-inch wheels wearing road-focused tyres, ABS as standard and has been engineered to accommodate two riders. An onboard Level 2 charger is also included, allowing the motorcycle to be plugged into compatible public charging points. Zero says the Ventura will be suitable for A1 licence holders in Europe, making it an option for younger riders as well as those looking to move into electric motorcycling. The company says the project has been developed with three priorities in mind: distinctive styling, an approachable riding experience for people familiar with electric bikes and e-motos, and a focus on making the finished motorcycle enjoyable to ride. Zero has stated that the new bike will be ready to ride by Summer 2027. signals.title: CFMOTO launches its first European scooter, and it's packed with tech
signals.summary: CFMOTO has revealed its first European-market scooter, with the new 125SC-S bringing a liquid-cooled 125cc engine, ABS, traction control and a generous helping of technology to the urban commuter segment. CFMOTO is expanding its European two-wheel line-up beyond motorcycles with the introduction of the new 125SC-S, a sporty-looking 125cc scooter aimed at urban and suburban commuters. The new model marks the Chinese manufacturer's debut in the European scooter market and has been developed around everyday practicality, with a focus on accessible performance, safety equipment and connectivity. Power comes from an all-new, in-house-developed 125cc liquid-cooled, four-valve single-cylinder engine. The company has yet to publish detailed performance figures, but says the unit has been designed to deliver smooth, responsive power alongside efficient operation in everyday riding conditions. Styling is a little more aggressive than some traditional commuter scooters, with sharp bodywork and distinctive twin-lens LED headlights giving the 125SC-S a sporty appearance. Its 780mm seat height should also make it accessible to a broad range of riders. Safety equipment includes dual-channel ABS and traction control, alongside high-intensity LED lighting and an Emergency Stop Signal system, which activates the brake lights under heavy braking to alert following traffic. There are two equipment levels, with the higher-specification version gaining gas-reservoir rear shock absorbers and heated grips. These additions should make the scooter more comfortable when dealing with poor road surfaces and colder weather. Practicality is another area CFMOTO has focused on, with 30 litres of under-seat storage providing enough room for a full-face helmet and an additional half helmet. There are also two enclosed front gloveboxes and USB charging for keeping devices powered while on the move. The cockpit features a 6.2-inch TFT display, while Bluetooth and NFC keyless access add further convenience. Connected functions and over-the-air software updates are also included in the technology package. The 125SC-S represents a new direction for CFMOTO in Europe, bringing the brand into a busy 125cc scooter market where established manufacturers already have a strong presence. Pricing, UK availability and full technical specifications have yet to be confirmed. signals.summary: CFMOTO has expanded its adventure range with two new 527cc models, offering a road-focused tourer and a more off-road-oriented machine based around the same parallel-twin engine. CFMOTO is adding two new models to its MT adventure range with the arrival of the 550MT and 550MT-X, two motorcycles that share the same engine but take rather different approaches to adventure riding. Both bikes are powered by a new 527cc parallel-twin engine producing 54hp at 8,500rpm and 52Nm (38.4lb-ft) of torque at 6,000rpm. However, while the standard 550MT has been developed with touring comfort and electronic rider aids in mind, the 550MT-X takes a more focused approach to off-road riding, with longer-travel suspension, larger wheels and a lighter overall package. The new engine represents a sizeable step up from the 450MT's 449cc unit, with CFMOTO claiming around 30 per cent more power. Both new models also feature a bi-directional quickshifter, although the standard 550MT goes a step further with an electronic clutch system designed to make everyday riding and gear changes easier. Of the two new arrivals, the 550MT-X is clearly the more dirt-focused machine. It uses a 21-inch front wheel and 18-inch rear wheel combination, alongside fully adjustable KYB suspension offering 230mm of travel at the front and 220mm at the rear. Ground clearance is set at 250mm, giving it the necessary dimensions for tackling more demanding terrain. CFMOTO claims a dry weight of 172kg and a ready-to-ride figure of 183kg, making it 3kg lighter than the 450MT despite the larger-capacity engine. The braking setup also differs from the standard model, with a single 320mm front disc used to help reduce unsprung weight. Its bodywork has been kept relatively compact, with a narrow waist and one-piece seat intended to make it easier for riders to move around when standing on the footpegs. These are all fairly conventional ingredients for a more serious adventure bike, but they give the 550MT-X a noticeably different brief to its road-oriented sibling. Electronics include selectable power modes and an Off-Road setting that allows traction control and rear-wheel ABS to be switched off. A standard bi-directional quickshifter is also included, alongside a vertically mounted 6.2-inch display with MotoPlay connectivity. The standard 550MT uses the same 527cc engine but takes a more touring-friendly approach to its chassis and equipment. Its 19-inch front and 17-inch rear wheels are more suited to predominantly road-based riding, while KYB suspension is fitted to provide a balance between comfort and everyday versatility. It also gets a more comprehensive electronics package, including three riding modes, IMU-based cornering ABS and traction control, cruise control and a Rear Detection System (RDS). The latter adds another layer of rider assistance, while an 8-inch MMI 2.0 display brings Apple CarPlay connectivity to the cockpit. The standard 550MT also gets an electronic clutch, Smart Key functionality and electronic access features, positioning it as the more convenience-focused of the two motorcycles. Touring practicality has been considered, too, with a 23-litre fuel tank and a two-piece seat. Seat height is adjustable between 800mm and 820mm, giving riders some flexibility when setting the bike up to suit their needs. Pricing, availability and full UK specifications for both motorcycles have yet to be confirmed. signals.title: CFMOTO takes aim at Ducati with new 210hp V4 superbike
signals.summary: CFMOTO's new V4-powered flagship brings active aerodynamics, a 15,000rpm engine and premium European components to the litre-class superbike market. CFMOTO is making no secret of its ambitions in the superbike market, with its new V4SR-RR arriving as the Chinese manufacturer's most technically advanced sportsbike to date. And while the styling might look familiar to anyone with an eye for Italian superbikes, the new machine has some interesting engineering of its own. Unveiled as part of CFMOTO's latest EICMA developments, the V4SR-RR is built around an in-house-developed 997cc, 90-degree V4 engine producing more than 210hp, according to the Chinese brand. That puts it within touching distance of the 218hp produced by Ducati's latest Panigale V4 S, despite the CFMOTO having a near 106cc capacity disadvantage. The comparison with Ducati is difficult to ignore. The V4SR-RR uses a front-frame chassis arrangement and a 90-degree V4 engine, with the overall engineering philosophy bearing more than a passing resemblance to the Panigale. Both manufacturers also use counter-rotating crankshafts, a configuration designed to help manage gyroscopic forces and improve the motorcycle's handling characteristics. However, CFMOTO has its own headline technology, particularly when it comes to aerodynamics. One of the most unusual features of the V4SR-RR is its active aerodynamic system, which uses independently operated winglets to alter the airflow around the front of the motorcycle. According to CFMOTO, the system can increase front-wheel downforce by 20 per cent immediately before braking at 160km/h, compared with conventional fixed winglets. The system can also operate asymmetrically at higher speeds to assist directional changes. The aerodynamic package is part of a wider performance-focused approach that includes fully adjustable chassis geometry and premium components from several established suppliers. Öhlins provides the suspension, while braking is handled by Brembo and it’s top-spec Hypure calipers. The bike also gets Pirelli Diablo Supercorsa SP V4 tyres and a full-titanium Akrapovič exhaust system. If anything, this signals CFMOTO’s official entry into the drool-worthy end of the motorcycle market. The 997cc V4 engine is claimed to produce more than 210hp and rev to 15,000rpm. It features titanium connecting rods manufactured by Pankl, alongside its counter-rotating crankshaft. CFMOTO quotes an approximate dry weight of 180kg, giving the V4SR-RR a claimed power-to-weight ratio that puts it firmly in the territory occupied by established 1,000cc plus superbikes. For comparison, Ducati's 2027 Panigale V4 S produces 218hp at 13,500rpm from its larger 1,103cc Desmosedici Stradale V4. Ducati quotes a weight of 187kg, although that figure is wet weight without fuel, so it cannot be directly compared with CFMOTO's dry-weight claim. The V4SR-RR will also be joined at EICMA by the V4SR-RR Carbon Black, a more track-focused interpretation of the new flagship. It features a selection of dedicated performance components and accessories, with CFMOTO describing it as a showcase for the platform's personalisation potential. Further details of the Carbon Black will be revealed at EICMA, with CFMOTO yet to provide a full production specification, pricing or availability information for the V4SR-RR. signals.title: Royal Enfield’s debut in the middleweight adventure class has arrived
signals.summary: Royal Enfield has officially unveiled its highly-anticipated Himalayan 750, which gets four variants and a UK price starting from £6,999. Royal Enfield has revealed its most powerful Himalayan to date as part of its 2027 model launch in Italy. The highly-anticipated launch of the Himalayan 750 had been on the cards for the best part of a year, after numerous spy shots emerged of the new model testing in India. The Himalayan 750 marks a significant moment in history for Royal Enfield, becoming one of two motorcycles to lead the marque into a new era. The Indian-owned company, which has been celebrating its 125-year anniversary throughout 2026, unveiled both bikes alongside various other motorcycles. The bike was presented at the EICMA show in Milan, Italy, and it will serve as the company’s flagship adventure bike above the Himalayan 450 and 411. The 2027 Himalayan 750 is powered by the all-new 743cc air/oil-cooled parallel-twin, producing a claimed 54bhp at 7,000rpm and 46.5 Ib-ft of torque at 5,000rpm, with 90 per cent of it available from as low as 3,500rpm. It comes with five riding modes; Road, Road Sport, Rain, Trail and Custom, a six-axis Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU), cornering ABS, lean-sensitive traction control, cruise control, and a 19/17-inch tubeless setup with cast or spoked wheels. Additionally, touring features such as an adjustable windscreen, independent rider and pillion seats, and a 195kg payload capacity make the Himalayan 750 Royal Enfield’s most adventurous model yet. Speaking about the new bike, B. Govindarajan, Managing Director - Eicher Motors Ltd., and Chief Executive Officer of Royal Enfield, said: “Leading our next chapter is the Himalayan 750, a motorcycle that builds on a decade of the Himalayan’s legacy. It brings greater capability, performance, and the perfect balance of technology, all while retaining the untamed spirit of exploration.” The new Himalayan 750 gets four variants in total, split across three different price brackets. Up first is the most affordable option in the range, which is the cast wheel option in Aztec Green at £6,999. From there, the spoked wheel option in Viking Bronze and Siberia White comes in at £7,299, while the top of the range Antarctic Silver option is fully loaded with bespoke luggage created in collaboration with GIVI. This particular model will cost £8,699. Suspension is handled by fully adjustable 43mm Showa USD forks with 190mm of travel, while a Showa monoshock with remote preload and rebound adjustment, offering 175mm of travel, is found at the rear. Two-piston brake calipers are paired with twin 280mm discs up front, while a single caliper bites down on a 255mm disc at the rear. According to Royal Enfield, seat height comes in at 815 and ground clearance at 205mm. The new adventure bike gets a 17.8-litre fuel tank, while the kerb weight is listed at 223kg. Information is fed via a 4-inch circular TFT dash with Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, navigation and phone controls. At the front of the bike, a 7-inch LED headlight is wrapped in an aluminium shell. signals.title: Superbike power wrapped in carbon fibre: BMW launches 218 hp M1000 RS
signals.summary: Limited to just 1,000 units worldwide, BMW is reshaping the hypernaked segment with this M1000 RR-powered M1000 RS. BMW is attempting to reshape the hypernaked segment through the reveal of the new M1000 RS, which is a stripped-back version of the company’s flagship superbike. At the heart of the new bike, which is limited to just 1,000 units worldwide, is the same inline four-cylinder engine that powers the M1000 RR. The M1000 RR is the machine used by BMW in the WorldSBK championship and in BSB, which also delivers 218 hp as a road-going motorcycle. The M1000 RS delivers its 218 hp (215bhp) at 14,500rpm alongside 83 Ib-ft of torque at 11,000rpm. But it’s not just the engine where the M1000 RR and M1000 RS share the same platform, as the former serves as the spiritual base for the new hypernaked. Meanwhile, the technical base is taken from the M1000 R in M Competition trim. The M rider footrest system is taken from the M1000 RR, while the bike’s seat height has been raised by 20mm. The new M1000 RS also receives the company’s top of the range M titanium exhaust system, as well as Matt carbon M winglets with RS lettering. Additionally, numerous Matt carbon components, a brushed aluminium fuel tank, new graphics and the Alcantara M seat complete the bike’s premium look. As standard features, the new bike gets heated grips, traction control, a detailed M start-up animation, Gearshift Assistant Pro, and Dynamic Damping Control (DDC). The suspension is handled by 45mm upside-down telescopic forks offering adjustable spring preload, and electronically controlled rebound and compression damping. The rear suspension features an aluminium underslung double-sided swingarm with adjustable preload, rebound and compression damping. Stopping power comes from BMW’s own M Competition package, with a four-piston caliper working alongside 320mm twin discs up front. At the rear is a 220mm single disc that’s paired with a single-piston caliper. Speaking about the new bike, BMW Motorrad CEO, Markus Flasch, said: “The BMW M 1000 RS makes a clear statement. RS stands for Rennsport – and that is exactly what you feel in every detail. With 218 hp, maximum precision and a character all its own, it is the world’s most powerful hyper naked bike. "And because true exclusivity needs limits, we are building exactly 1,000 units. More performance. More character. It simply does not get more M than this.” BMW says the new hypernaked weighs 196kg as a road-ready, fully fueled bike, while the fuel tank capacity is a claimed 16.5 litres. The BMW M1000 RS will be available in the UK with a price of £36,220. signals.title: Driven by the people: Yamaha reveals a new concept that customers are craving
signals.summary: Yamaha’s 2027 new-model launch at EICMA has given us more than just that, after the company revealed an exciting new Ténéré 4 Concept, driven by customer demand. Yamaha is set to give the people what they want, quite literally, after the new Ténéré 4 Concept was revealed on the eve of the EICMA show in Milan, Italy. According to Yamaha, the new concept has been driven by customer demand, and it is set for production as a lightweight A2-compliant model. But more importantly, this marks a huge step closer to Yamaha offering customers a more accessible entry point into the world of adventure riding, with its range currently dominated by the different Ténéré 7 bikes. The new Ténéré 4 Concept was showcased as part of an official ceremony alongside the all-new RW700, RW700 Explore and RW350. The Ténéré 4 Concept was unveiled by President of Yamaha Motor Europe, Olivier Prevost, who was joined on stage by off-road racers Pol Tarres and Kevin Galles. Yamaha has yet to confirm when the Ténéré 4 will move from being a concept model to a production-ready motorcycle. What we do know is that the new Ténéré 4 Concept is instantly recognisable as part of the Ténéré family thanks to its flat, low fuel-tank silhouette and narrow profile. It clearly pays homage to Yamaha’s rally roots, while also combining functional technology with robust engineering and a purposeful design, which has, unsurprisingly, been developed from Yamaha’s Adventure experience with the Ténéré 700. The Ténéré 4 Concept was presented with KYB suspension both front and rear, while its 21/18-inch spoked wheels were fitted with Michelin Anakee Wild tyres. Completing the look was a titanium Akrapovič exhaust. With a heavy focus on rider-led ergonomics, the Ténéré 4 Concept aims to deliver the “agility and accessibility expected from a new-generation Adventure motorcycle, while staying true to the decades long history of Yamaha’s Adventure segment”, says the Japanese brand. signals.title: You can have your cake and eat it: New GSX-10R, the best of both 1,000cc sportsbike
signals.summary: Suzuki has revealed the GSX-10R, a new 150bhp, 999cc sports bike with a K5-derived engine, advanced electronics and chassis development aimed at road and track riding. Suzuki has taken the covers off the GSX-10R, a new litre-class sports bike designed to offer a more usable alternative to the increasingly track-focused superbike formula. Built around a 999cc four-cylinder engine with roots in the much-loved K5 GSX-R1000, the GSX-10R combines serious sports bike hardware with a chassis and electronics package developed to work as well on the public road as it does on track. Suzuki is keen to position the GSX-10R as a bike for riders who enjoy sports riding without necessarily wanting the uncompromising nature of a dedicated homologation-level superbike. The company says it has been developed around the idea of enjoying a motorcycle across a range of environments, from commuting and weekend rides to touring and track sessions. In its own words, the GSX-10R is intended to be a different kind of GSX-R, rather than a machine chasing outright performance at the expense of everyday usability. At its heart is a 999cc, liquid-cooled, DOHC inline-four, based on the K5 engine architecture and further refined through the GSX-S1000. Suzuki has made changes to the exhaust valve specifications and cam chain assembly to improve reliability and reduce noise, while revising the engine's characteristics following testing on both circuits and public roads. The result is a claimed 150bhp at 11,000rpm and 78lb-ft of torque at 9,250rpm, with the engine meeting Euro 5+ emissions requirements. A ride-by-wire throttle and three selectable power modes allow riders to tailor the delivery, while a bi-directional quickshifter and slipper clutch are also fitted. Electronics are a major part of the GSX-10R package, with Suzuki's Intelligent Ride System incorporating 15 control systems. Among the headline additions is Suzuki's first slide control system, which works alongside traction control to detect and manage lateral movement of the rear tyre during cornering. The system is designed to allow a degree of controlled sliding while stepping in if the situation becomes more difficult to manage. Other equipment includes launch control, engine brake control, a lift limiter, cornering ABS and cruise control with curve speed control. There's also a new brake hold system, which can operate on flat ground and slopes. The GSX-10R sits on an aluminium twin-spar frame with a newly designed aluminium swingarm, while the suspension comes from KYB. The 43mm inverted front forks are fully adjustable, while the rear linkage-type shock allows adjustment of preload, rebound and high- and low-speed compression damping. Suzuki says the setup has been developed to offer a balance between circuit performance and comfort on the road. Braking is handled by twin front discs with a radial master cylinder, while the bike runs on Bridgestone Battlax Hypersport S23 tyres, in 120/70ZR17 front and 190/55ZR17 rear sizes. Suzuki also quotes a maximum lean angle of 53 degrees, five degrees more than the GSX-S1000. Despite its sporty intentions, the GSX-10R gets a fairly substantial 18-litre fuel tank and a newly developed seat designed to allow movement during spirited riding while offering more comfort on longer journeys. The forward-leaning riding position is described as equivalent to that of the GSX-R1000R, although Suzuki says the seat has softer padding than its flagship superbike. A full-colour TFT display, smartphone connectivity through the Suzuki Ride Connect+ app and a USB Type-C socket are also included. Styling takes obvious inspiration from the GSX-R family, with forward-swept winglets integrated into the fairing and three colour options: blue and silver, red and grey, and black and grey. The new bike tips the scales at 214kg (claimed kerb weight), has a seat height of 810mm and a wheelbase of 1,455mm. Suzuki has not included UK pricing or availability details in the launch information, but we’ll update that as soon as we have it. signals.title: Suzuki SV-7S brings new tech to the familiar SV650 V-twin
signals.summary: Just when you thought the SV650 had shuffled off this mortal coil, Suzuki has dragged it back for another go. Meet the SV-7S, the latest incarnation of a V-twin that simply refuses to die. The Suzuki SV650 really doesn't want to retire, does it? Having already been given a new lease of life in the shape of the SV-7GX, the Japanese manufacturer has now introduced another motorcycle built around its long-serving 645cc V-twin, this time in the form of the new SV-7S. While the SV-7GX takes the familiar SV formula in a more commuting and touring-focused direction, the SV-7S sticks much closer to the traditional naked roadster recipe. Think of it as the spiritual successor to the SV650, albeit one that has finally been dragged, somewhat reluctantly perhaps, into the modern electronic age. The engine is the same familiar liquid-cooled, 90-degree V-twin that has been at the heart of the SV family since 1999. Suzuki says more than 500,000 examples of the engine have been produced, and while it has undergone plenty of revisions over the years, the basic 645cc configuration remains. For the SV-7S, it produces 72bhp at 8,500rpm and 47.2lb-ft of torque at 6,800rpm, putting it on broadly the same performance footing as the SV-7GX. The engine has been updated with electronic throttle bodies, a revised airbox and a new 2-into-1 exhaust system, with the changes also helping it meet Euro 5+ regulations. There are some more substantial changes beneath the familiar mechanical foundations, though, with the introduction of Suzuki's ride-by-wire throttle system opening the door to a more comprehensive electronics package. The SV-7S comes equipped with Suzuki's Intelligent Ride System (S.I.R.S.), which includes three selectable riding modes, traction control with three intervention settings and an off option, and a bi-directional quickshifter. The riding modes are split into A, B and C settings, with the first offering the sharpest throttle response, B providing a more balanced delivery for everyday use, and C softening things off for improved controllability. Interestingly, the C setting also limits maximum power to 45kW, making it suitable for A2 riders, although not in the legal sense, as the bike can return to full power at the flick of a switch. The quickshifter allows clutchless upshifts above 2,000rpm and downshifts above 1,700rpm, while Suzuki's Low RPM Assist and Easy Start systems are also fitted. There's a new 4.2-inch colour TFT display, too, which provides smartphone connectivity through Suzuki Ride Connect+. This brings turn-by-turn navigation, call and message notifications, weather information and traffic alerts to the instrument panel, alongside the usual riding information. Where the SV-7GX adopts a crossover-style silhouette, the SV-7S goes back to the traditional naked roadster look, complete with a new round LED headlight, exposed trellis frame and relatively slim bodywork. The chassis is based around a tubular steel trellis frame, with a 41mm telescopic fork offering 125mm of travel and a rear monoshock providing 129mm. The latter features seven-step preload adjustment, while braking comes courtesy of twin 290mm front discs with four-piston calipers and a single 240mm rear disc, supported by two-channel ABS. The bike runs on 17-inch cast aluminium wheels, wrapped in Dunlop Roadsmart III tyres measuring 120/70ZR17 at the front and 160/60ZR17 at the rear. Interestingly, the SV-7S is a little more compact than its crossover sibling. It has a 785mm seat height, compared with the SV-7GX's 795mm, while kerb weight is quoted at 200kg, some 11kg less than the GX. The fuel tank is also smaller, holding 14 litres rather than the crossover's 17.4 litres. The wheelbase remains the same at 1,445mm, as does the 25-degree rake and 106mm trail, suggesting the two machines share much of their underlying chassis architecture. Suzuki will offer the SV-7S in three colour combinations: Pearl Suzuki Deep Blue No.4 with a silver frame, Glass Sparkle Black with a grey frame, and Mat Sword Silver with black body panels. The headline figures include a claimed fuel consumption of 4.1 litres per 100km, equivalent to around 68.9mpg and giving the bike a usable tank range of around 100 miles. At this stage, UK pricing and availability have not been confirmed; we’ll update this page when that happens. The arrival of the SV-7S gives Suzuki another way of keeping its long-running V-twin relevant, and one that arguably makes more sense for traditional SV650 fans than the more touring-oriented SV-7GX. With the familiar engine, conventional naked styling and a much-needed injection of electronic assistance, the SV650's retirement plans appear to have been postponed once again. signals.title: Watch out Honda: Yamaha launches CP2-powered RW700 adventure scooter
signals.summary: Yamaha has launched a new adventure scooter range featuring two Honda rivals, including the radical RW700 which is powered by the company’s 689cc CP2 parallel twin. Yamaha has revealed a completely new line-up for 2027 as it looks to muscle its way into the adventure scooter market. The Iwata-based brand is bringing three radical new models to the table, including the range-topping RW700 and RW700 Explore. The RW700 and RW700 Explore are both fitted with the company’s proven 689cc CP2 parallel twin, and its six-speed Y-AMT (Yamaha Automated Manual Transmission) system, allowing riders to change gears via a switch on the left handlebar. The Y-AMT system was first introduced by Yamaha in 2024, and can now be found on numerous models within its motorcycle line-up, including the MT-09 and MT-07, and across its Tracer 9 GT family. Both models also feature the Yamaha Chip Controlled Throttle (YCC-T) system, aimed at delivering smoother torque throughout the entire rev range. Yamaha claims a maximum power of 51 kW (68.4bhp) at 8,250rpm and 48 Ib-ft of torque at 6,750rpm. The RW700 and RW700 Explore are also available as A2 machines, where power is restricted to 47bhp. Both scooters are available with two colour options, with the standard RW700 receiving Sage Blue and Power Grey variants. Meanwhile, the RW700 Explore gets Forest Green and Midnight Black options. Thanks to the six-axis IMU system, both models feature a full suite of electronic rider aids, including traction control, slide control and brake control. Additionally, the company’s Yamaha Ride Control (YRC) allows the rider to select different engine power characteristics as well as changing the level of support from the electronic rider aids, based on personal rider preferences. There are numerous riding modes available which have been split into two categories: Road and Gravel. Road consists of three modes including Sport, Street and Eco, while Gravel allows the rider to choose between Explore and Explore+. The latter provides more engine feedback than Explore. The two RW700 models are separated by their level of trim, with the higher-spec Explore gaining a front suspension setup that features adjustable preload and rebound damping capabilities, heated grips, heated seat, a centre stand and backlit switchgear. The 41mm inverted forks are the same on both models, providing 160mm of front wheel travel. They are paired with a bottom-link type monoshock with 155mm travel at the rear with adjustable seven-step preload. The RW700 Explore gives extra rider control with 15mm of front fork preload adjustability and 11-step rebound damping adjustability. Both models gain an autoshift-compatible cruise control system plus Yamaha Variable Speed Limiter (YVSL). Finally, smart key technology complements a connectivity-ready five-inch TFT display and USB-C socket. At the heart of the smaller RW350 is a brand-new 327cc liquid cooled single-cylinder engine, producing 28.8bhp at 7,000rpm and 23.2 Ib-ft of torque at 5,750rpm. According to Yamaha, “the newly developed engine is part of a unique layout unlike anything Yamaha have used before: Yamaha Dynamic Ride. Unlike unit-swing setups where the engine and CVT housing are integrated and move vertically as a single unit, or rigid mounting arrangements where the swingarm extends rearward from the engine with the CVT unit fixed to the frame, Yamaha Dynamic Ride offers a setup where the engine is fixed to the frame, while only the CVT unit moves vertically around the crankshaft pivot”. The new engine also features the same Yamaha Chip Controlled Throttle (YCC-T) that’s found aboard the bigger RW700 models, which is another first for Yamaha in this class. Suspension is handled by 37mm inverted forks at the front with 140mm of travel, and twin shocks at the rear allowing 105mm. The suspension is also adjustable across seven settings, therefore it can be tuned to suit road conditions, or the weight of having a passenger or luggage on the bike. Specific to the RW350 is the wheel design, which is inspired by rally car wheels with a large dish shape around the hub. Another first for Yamaha is the cast aluminium rear wheel which houses a damper inside the hub. This is designed to reduce vibration during both acceleration and deceleration. The 16-inch front wheel is paired with the 14-inch rear, with the RW350 sporting Dunlop D615 tubeless block-pattern tyres developed specifically for this particular model. It’s clear that the RW700 arrives as a direct competitor to Honda’s X-ADV, while the smaller RW350 will act as a rival to the ADV350. signals.title: Honda unleashes its race DNA with its new flagship superbike for 2027
signals.summary: After operating as Honda’s flagship superbike since 2024, the new CBR1000RR-R Fireblade SP is getting a plethora of meaningful changes to make it a contender for the best-in-class. Inspired by its WorldSBK project, the brand-new 2027 Honda CBR1000RR-R Fireblade SP has gained a series of changes to take on Ducati’s mighty Panigale V4. The engine layout remains the same as before, meaning the 2027 Fireblade SP retains its 1,000cc inline four-cylinder power unit, producing 160kW (214.6bhp) at 14,000rpm and 114Nm (84.1lb-ft) at 10,500rpm. That being said, there are a list of revisions to the engine that have been made, including new cam timing, expanded cam timing adjustment capability and updates to the valve train. Additionally, newly machined piston crowns and combustion chambers mean the compression ratio has been raised, while engine covers made from magnesium, aluminium fasteners and lighter crankcases have led to reduced mass. The crankshaft centreline has also been raised, while a revised mainshaft and countershaft spacing allow for a wider transmission ratio. First gear is now five per cent taller than the outgoing Fireblade SP, although the titanium Akrapovič muffler remains unchanged from before. The SP model is a higher-spec version of the standard CBR1000RR-R, which is also new for 2027 alongside the HRC Works Edition. All of this has resulted in a three-head superbike monster from Honda, and the message from its EICMA launch is clear: Honda wants to be the best-in-class with regards to the superbike segment. As a road bike, some people may already view the CBR1000RR-R as that, others might prefer the Panigale V4, which in the form of the R model, is currently the undisputed king of racing. The BMW M1000 RR is another rival of the CBR1000RR-R Fireblade SP which ranks close to the top in some minds. But for Honda, the new CBR1000RR-R Fireblade SP marks a huge leap forward as it has been developed with racing in mind first, and the road second. It has been inspired and developed through HRC’s racing lens, which is backed by decades of competing at the top of both MotoGP and WorldSBK. The new model is supported by an all-new aluminium frame, which has a revised rigidity philosophy and new steering geometry, and is paired with a lighter swingarm. Öhlins Smart Electronic Control 43mm NPX forks are paired with a TTX36 rear shock that’s operated by Öhlins Object Based Tuning interface (OBTi). The wheels are also new, featuring a lighter design than before, which is also true of the 330mm front discs, as well as new Brembo Hypure four-piston front calipers. Continuing with what’s new aboard the company’s flagship Fireblade SP, a completely new aero package has been introduced, while the fairing retains the same downforce levels of the previous model with a cleaner new styling. The new LED headlight features Daytime Running Lights (DRL), while the titanium fuel tank is now exposed, and the seat height raised. The new CBR1000RR-R Fireblade SP will be available in two colourways; Ignition Red and Mat Ballistic Black Metallic.
